summary: SuperHumans is a crew-health instrument for astronauts: six AI health checks that run on real medical data inside the browser, and each one ends in what to do next. TrackTrace circles DNA damage in a cell nucleus and looks for the straight track of a heavy ion. BubbleGrade listens to heart Doppler sound after a spacewalk and grades the gas bubbles behind the bends. SpikeCount outlines every red blood cell in a microscope photo and grades the spiky shapes linked to space anemia. VeinSqueeze reads a vein-ultrasound clip for a clot. BrainDrift maps a brain MRI and measures the upward shift and fluid swelling seen after long flights. Garn Meter tracks space sickness. Far from Earth, a crew cannot wait for a specialist on the ground. SuperHumans puts the first reading, and the next step, in the crew's own hands. We trained the models ourselves during the hackathon on open data, including NASA's own microscopy of irradiated cells, and the checks run in the browser with no server.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

On a Mars mission a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to 20 minutes to arrive, and the answer as long again. SuperHumans is built for that gap. It gives an astronaut six health checks, each made for a problem that spaceflight really causes, and each one ends in a plain sentence: who acts, and what to do next.

1. TrackTrace: radiation. A heavy cosmic-ray ion crosses a cell in a straight line and breaks DNA along its path. Our own model, IonScan, looks at a microscope image of one cell nucleus, circles every DNA-damage spot, and draws a line when the spots fall in a row. A second small model reads a whole sample of several hundred nuclei and gives one verdict: which radiation, which dose band, how long ago.

2. BubbleGrade: the bends. After a spacewalk in a low-pressure suit, gas bubbles can form in the blood. BubbleGrade listens to Doppler ultrasound sound recorded over the heart and grades the bubbles on the Spencer scale (0 to IV), the scale used in NASA's decompression chamber trials. It shows the sound it heard and where in the clip the bubble-like sound was.

3. SpikeCount: space anemia. In orbit the body destroys more red blood cells. SpikeCount outlines every red cell in a blood-smear photo, grades its shape from smooth disc to spiky ball, and compares the share of spiky cells with the astronaut's own pre-flight sample.

4. VeinSqueeze: blood clots. The first blood clot found in space, in an astronaut's neck vein on the ISS, was confirmed with a squeeze test: a healthy vein squashes flat under the ultrasound probe, a vein with a clot stays round. VeinSqueeze reads a compression-ultrasound clip and gives a clot probability as an AI second opinion.

5. BrainDrift: the floating brain. On long missions the brain shifts upward in the skull and its fluid spaces swell. BrainDrift colours every point of a brain MRI by tissue type, measures the fluid spaces and the height of the brain's top, and reports the change between two scans.

6. Garn Meter: space sickness, in "Garns", a joke unit from astronaut folklore: one Garn is as sick as it gets. CorrFuse-EEG, a brainwave (EEG) model we trained, reads a recorded session and the gauge shows its reading. It is an experimental model: on new people it is barely better than chance yet, and the app marks it experimental.

HOW IT WORKS

Each check is a neural network that we trained during the hackathon on openly published research data, then exported to a small file that runs inside the web browser on the device's own graphics chip. There is no server and nothing is uploaded: the page downloads the model and the reading happens on the laptop. On phones the checks replay stored outputs of the same models, and the page says so. The same code can also run as a desktop app (Electron).

Every check follows the same three steps. First the real sample fills the screen: the nucleus, the heart sound, the blood cells, the ultrasound clip, the brain. Then one press runs the model, and what it found is drawn on the sample itself. Last comes one answer and the next step, with who should act: the astronaut, the crew medical officer, or the flight surgeon on the ground. Any result that needs action says that a human reviews it; Garn Meter, being experimental, shows only its reading. Under each check, the page tells the problem with real imagery and then shows the model's architecture, drawn from the code we shipped.

IonScan, the model behind TrackTrace, is our own design. It cuts the image of a nucleus into a 32 by 32 grid and reads it along four directions, each both ways, with a selective state-space memory, a little like a particle detector adding up hits along a path. Attention layers follow. It has 3.19 million parameters. We trained it on NASA's BPS Microscopy benchmark: 77,177 mouse cell nuclei from NASA Open Science study OSD-366, irradiated on the ground with an iron-ion beam or with X-rays, or left unirradiated.

WHAT WE MEASURED

All results are on data the models never saw during training.

- TrackTrace: its count of damage spots agrees with the counts in NASA's dataset (Spearman 0.954; spot F1 0.920) on 3 unseen mice. The whole-sample verdict is right for 97% of samples on radiation type, 88% on dose band and 95% on time since exposure (34 samples). Per single nucleus, the radiation-type score is 0.674 (macro-F1); a standard MobileNetV4 network scores 0.678.

- BubbleGrade: trained and tested on 6,826 recordings from 310 divers. Its spacewalk alert flags 87% of grade III-IV clips at 70% specificity (AUROC 0.892).

- SpikeCount: its share of spiky cells per photo tracks the experts' (r 0.933, average error 4.57 percentage points); cell outlines F1 0.948.

- VeinSqueeze: AUC 0.785 pooled over 594 patients, 0.720 within one scanner brand. That is modest, so it is shown as a second opinion for screening and never as a diagnosis.

- BrainDrift: fluid-space outlines match the reference at Dice 0.953 on 40 unseen brains, and volume agrees at r 0.999. On a simulated flight it measures the change to within 1.03 percentage points on average.

- Garn Meter: the brainwave model scores AUROC 0.54 on new people, barely above chance (0.50). The standard EEG network we raced against it scores 0.56. The app shows the model's reading on the gauge, marked as an experimental model, and we report this result here as it is.

WHAT IT IS NOT

No astronaut data is public, so every model learned from ground stand-ins: mouse cells under an accelerator beam, divers, lab blood from healthy donors, hospital leg-vein scans, brain MRI of people on Earth, and a virtual-reality sickness study. The brain "flight" is a simulation built from two published numbers. In TrackTrace, part of the difference the model sees between iron ions and X-rays comes from lab batch; the spot count and the whole-sample call are what we trust. SuperHumans does not diagnose anything. It is a working prototype of how a crew could take a first reading and know the next step. The decision thresholds are our own product rules; the actions come from NASA documents and clinical practice, each cited in the app.

BENEFITS

- Autonomy: a first reading and a next step on board, without waiting for Earth.

- One instrument across the hazards NASA's Human Research Program names: radiation, pressure change on spacewalks, and the fluid shifts of weightlessness.

- No server: everything runs on an ordinary laptop, and medical data never leaves the device.

- On Earth, the same approach suits places where a specialist is far away: ships, polar stations, remote clinics.

- Honest by design: each check shows what it measured, how well it works and where it fails.

WHAT IS NEXT

- Accept raw files from real instruments (microscope images, MRI volumes, EEG recordings) and not only our prepared samples.

- Test BubbleGrade on modern Doppler probes; our one test on modern recordings failed, so we make no claim there.

- Better personal calibration for the Garn Meter brainwave model: one calibration session per person raised it to AUROC 0.62, but it still missed our own pass marks.

- Align real before-and-after brain scans; today the flight is simulated.

- Measure speed on phones so more checks can run live there.

- Work with flight-medicine experts on the thresholds, which today are our own rules.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE

Website and desktop app: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, ONNX Runtime Web (WebGPU with a WebAssembly fallback), Electron. Model training: Python, PyTorch, timm and nnU-Net, on rented cloud GPUs (Google Colab). Open pretrained models used as starting points or helpers: MobileNetV4 (ImageNet weights from timm), the OpenMind brain-MRI encoder, SAM 2.1 and HD-BET. The code of the website and the app is open source under the MIT licence: https://github.com/Kreytorn/superhumans. Every dataset, model, library, font and tool is credited with its licence in THIRD_PARTY.md in that repository.
